title: Prophecy needs preparation
hook: prophecy requires mind, character and imagination

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the hand is a metaphor. The strong hand points at power, the eyes at care. Which body word did you catch yourself using today? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

Three kings and their armies are stuck in a desert with no water, and they come to the prophet Elisha for a word from God. He has hard words for one of them, the king of Israel. Then he asks for something odd. Not a scroll, not an altar. A musician. "But now bring me a minstrel." The musician plays, and the text says the hand of the LORD came upon him, and he speaks. Why would a prophet need music first? Maimonides has an answer, and today's word is the heart of it.
screen: `NO WATER IN THE DESERT.` → `ELISHA'S HARD WORDS.` → `BRING ME A MINSTREL.`

segments.voice: Prophecy needs preparation. Turn it four ways. First, the mind. In his law code Maimonides writes that prophecy rests only on a person great in wisdom, strong in character, whose impulses never overpower them. In the Guide he explains why: prophecy flows from God first into a person's reasoning mind. A mind that hasn't been trained has nowhere to hold it. Second, character. A person ruled by appetite, by greed, by the hunger for honor, is pulled in too many directions to receive anything. So the work on character we saw earlier in his Eight Chapters, the middle way, isn't a separate subject. It's part of the same preparation. Third, imagination. This is the surprising one. Maimonides says prophecy then flows into the imagination, which is why prophets see visions, parables and dreams, not lectures. A philosopher with a strong mind but a weak imagination might understand deeply and still not be a prophet. And imagination is fragile. He says sadness and anger shut it down, which is how he reads Elisha: angered, he needed the music to bring back joy and calm before prophecy could come. Fourth, the limit. Does all this preparation guarantee prophecy? No. Maimonides holds that even a fully prepared person may not receive it, if God withholds it. Preparation doesn't force the gift. It makes a person able to hold it. For him, that's the line between a vessel and a demand.
screen: `A TRAINED MIND.` · `A STEADY CHARACTER.` · `A LIVELY IMAGINATION.` · `READY IS NOT GUARANTEED.` · then, large: `PREPARE THE VESSEL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and breathe. Run through the three faculties Maimonides names, and check in on each one. The mind: is it rested, or scattered today? Character: is anything pulling hard right now, irritation, wanting, worry? Imagination: is there room in you for a picture, a song, a vision of something better? Pick the one that needs the most care. Then choose one small thing for it. A page of real reading for the mind. Letting go of one grudge for character. A piece of music for the imagination, the way Elisha asked. The bell holds the time.

Prophecy needs preparation. Maimonides' teaching that prophecy comes only to someone with a trained mind, a steady character and a strong imagination, and even then only as God gives it. Today's word.
Your line: prepare the vessel. Today, do the one small thing you chose for your mind, your character or your imagination, before the day fills up. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews who study Maimonides read his account of prophecy in the Laws of the Foundations of the Torah, chapter seven, and in the second part of the Guide. Tradition holds that prophecy has ceased, so the teaching is studied as a picture of human readiness.

fork.setup: you're Elisha. three kings want a word from God, and you've just spoken hard words to one of them. what do you do?
options: speak at once, angry or not.
ask for a musician to play first.
fork.reveal: he says, 'but now bring me a minstrel.' when the music plays, the hand of the LORD comes upon him.

original.note: Hebrew: prophecy. Maimonides' term for what flows to a prepared mind and imagination.

trapdoor: what you thought: God picks prophets at random, out of nowhere.
what it means: prophecy needs a trained mind, steady character and strong imagination, and still comes only as God gives it.
what a scholar hears: Guide 2:32 and 2:36, Yesodei HaTorah 7:1, and Elisha's minstrel in 2 Kings 3:15 read as calming anger.

sources.quoted: But now bring me a minstrel.

notes: 2 Kings 3:15 quoted as JPS 1917; please confirm exact wording. The scene (the kings of Israel, Judah and Edom, no water, Elisha's anger at the king of Israel) is paraphrased from 3:9–14; the hook says 'three kings', which the chapter supports; please confirm.

Yesodei HaTorah 7:1 (wise, strong in character, impulses not overpowering) and 7:4 (sadness and anger prevent prophecy) paraphrased. Guide 2:36 (emanation to the rational then imaginative faculty; sadness and anger; Elisha's minstrel) and 2:32 (God may withhold prophecy from the prepared) paraphrased. Please confirm.

Editor: 2 Kings 3 shows Elisha rebuking the king of Israel but does not say he was angry; the narrator now says 'hard words', and anger is attributed only to Maimonides' reading (Guide 2:36, after Pesachim 66b). Hook screen, myth and fork adjusted to match.
